Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Psychiatry, Hospital Universitario Rey Juan Carlos, Móstoles, Spain. * 2 Department of Psychology and Sociology, Area of Personality, Assessment and Psychological Treatment, Universidad of Zaragoza, Teruel, Spain. * 3 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Hospital 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain. inmaculada.penuelas@salud.madrid.org. * 4 Department of Legal Medicine, Psychiatry and Pathology, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain. inmaculada.penuelas@salud.madrid.org. * 5 Department of Psychiatry, Hospital Universitario Fundación Jiménez Díaz, Madrid, Spain. * 6 Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Fundación Jiménez Díaz, Madrid, Spain. * 7 Division of Psychiatry, Imperial College, London, UK. * 8 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Hospital 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain. * 9 Department of Legal Medicine, Psychiatry and Pathology, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain. * 10 Department of Psychiatry, Hospital Universitario Infanta Elena, Valdemoro, Madrid, Spain. * 11 Department of Psychiatry, Hospital Universitario Central de Villalba, Madrid, Spain. * 12 Universidad Católica del Maule, Talca, Chile. * 13 CIBERSAM, Madrid, Spain. * 14 Université de Nîmes, Nîmes, France. * 15 Department of Psychiatry, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, Madrid, Spain. * 16 Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Fundación Jiménez Díaz, Madrid, Spain. alexposeg@gmail.com. * 17 Division of Psychiatry, Imperial College, London, UK. alexposeg@gmail.com. * PMID: 37470845 * DOI: 10.1007/s00787-023-02260-2 Abstract There might be differential characteristics between those who have attempted suicide once in their lifetime (single attempters) and those who have attempted suicide two or more times (multiple attempters). This study was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and the review protocol was registered in PROSPERO. We conducted a systematic literature search in three databases to identify original studies exploring the characteristics of single attempters vs. multiple attempters among adolescents. We considered a wide range for the definition of adolescent, following most recent recommendations: 10-24 years. We carried out a meta-analysis. Fourteen studies were included in the systematic review and 13 in the meta-analysis with a total sample of with a total of 4286 participants. The factors statistically significantly associated with being a multiple attempter in the meta-analysis were: anxiety disorders, depression severity, alcohol abuse, substance abuse, aggressiveness, and hopelessness. Multiple attempters have a more severe clinical profile, with greater severity of symptoms. Knowledge of the risk factors associated with being a multiple attempter could help us to predict which patients are more likely to reattempt suicide and need further monitoring and a tailored treatment. Prevention programs tailored for the adolescent population, along with identification of early risk factors, could help to prevent suicidal behavior among this vulnerable population. Published in final edited form as: Suicide Life Threat Behav. 2017 Aug 22;48(5):580–588. doi: 10.1111/sltb.12375 Abstract The present study examined a conceptual model in which the association between aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation is moderated by internalizing symptoms and ongoing stress. Participants were 304 psychiatric inpatient adolescents (65.8% girls) ranging in age from 12 to 17 years (Mean age = 14.69). The association between aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation was significantly moderated by internalizing symptoms and ongoing stress; the association was positive in adolescents low in internalizing symptoms or high in ongoing stress, but negative in adolescents high in internalizing symptoms or low in ongoing stress. The three-way interaction between aggressive behaviors, internalizing symptoms, and ongoing stress was not statistically significant. The current findings indicate that in adolescents who display high levels of aggressive behaviors, the presence of high ongoing stress provides a more useful indicator of levels of suicide ideation than the presence of high internalizing symptoms. implications for case identification and prevention are discussed. ---------------------------------------- Seventeen percent of high school students reported seriously considering a suicide attempt and 14% reported making a specific plan about how they would attempt suicide in the past 12 months (CDC, 2014). A much higher percentage of adolescents in psychiatric hospitals experience suicide ideation, with estimates ranging from 40% to 80% (e.g., Venta & Sharp, 2014). The high prevalence of suicide ideation in adolescence highlights the need for research on variables that are associated with and may contribute to its occurrence. Past research on suicide ideation has focused heavily on internalizing symptoms, including symptoms of depression and anxiety, and has documented significant associations between these symptoms and suicide ideation in adolescents (e.g., Hill, Castellanos, & Pettit, 2011; Lewinsohn, Rohde, & Seeley, 1996). In light of these documented associations, case identification and prevention approaches for suicide-related behaviors often prioritize internalizing symptoms (e.g., Aseltine & DeMartino, 2004; King, Berona, Czyz, Horwitz, & Gipson, 2015). However, there also is evidence that suicidal crises may develop in a subset of individuals who experience low levels of internalizing symptoms (e.g., Cukrowicz et al., 2011; Kerr et al., 2007). Identification of variables that are associated with suicide ideation in individuals who show low levels of internalizing symptoms is important to refine and improve case identification strategies and prevention programs. Preliminary evidence suggests that this subset of individuals, especially in adolescence, is characterized by high levels of aggressive behaviors (Kerr et al., 2007; Simon et al., 2001). For example, Simon et al. (2001) found that a subset of suicide attempters who made attempts with minimal planning also had histories of aggressive behaviors (i.e., physical fighting). This finding is consistent with the possibility that adolescents who experience high levels of aggressive behaviors may be at risk for suicide ideation even in the context of low levels of ongoing internalizing symptoms. Stated differently, among adolescents who are high in aggressive behaviors, it is possible that ongoing internalizing symptoms are not good indicators of suicide risk (cf. Kerr et al., 2007). This possibility is consistent with the Three Step Theory (i.e., ideation to action framework) that emphasizes emotional and/or physical pain in the development of suicide ideation (Klonsky & May, 2015; May & Klonsky, 2016). Aggressive adolescents tend to experience high levels of emotionally painful yet transient states, including anger, frustration, and intense emotion dysregulation (e.g., Fives, Kong, Fuller, & Digiuseppe, 2011; McLaughlin, Hatzenbuehler, Mennin, & Nolen-Hoeksema, 2011), that differ from ongoing high levels of internalizing symptoms. If internalizing symptoms are not good indicators of suicide risk among adolescents who are high in aggression, it would have important implications for case identification and prevention approaches. Namely, the focus on internalizing symptoms to screen adolescents could miss a portion of adolescents who experience suicide ideation and are at risk for severe suicide-related behaviors. Screening programs may need to include aggressive behaviors to provide a more sensitive approach to identifying adolescents who experience suicide ideation. Further, for this subset of adolescents, targeting internalizing symptoms such as depression and anxiety may not be the optimal approach for preventing suicide ideation. Rather, for this subset, prevention and intervention efforts may be more impactful if they target aggressive behaviors (Newcomer et al., 2015). Results After age 17-18, the majority of suicide attempts were repeat attempts (i.e., made by individuals with prior suicidal behavior). Intent increased both with increasing age, and with number of prior attempts. Medical lethality increased as a function of age but not recurrent attempts. The time between successive suicide attempts decreased as a function of number of attempts. The amount of precipitating life stress was not related to attempts. Conclusions Adolescents and young adults show evidence of escalation of recurrent suicidal behavior, with increasing suicidal intent and decreasing time between successive attempts. However, evidence that sensitization processes account for this escalation was inconclusive. For example, in community and population-based studies, the transition to adolescence has been found to be associated with a marked increase in the rates of suicide attempts (Boeninger, Masyn, Feldman, & Conger, 2010; Joffe, Offord, & Boyle, 1988; Kessler, Borges, & Walters, 1999; Lewinsohn, Rohde, Seeley, & Baldwin, 2001; Velez & Cohen, 1988; Wunderlich et al., 2001). Females generally attempt suicide at higher rates than males (Lewinsohn et al., 2001; Nock et al., 2013), and in one study, the increase in suicide attempts during adolescence was found primarily among females (Lewinsohn et al., 2001). In community samples, the rate of suicide attempts has been observed to decline during the transition to young adulthood (Kessler et al., 1999; Lewinsohn et al., 2001). Fewer studies have examined age trends in suicide attempts in clinical or high-risk samples, but results suggest similar patterns in the prevalence of suicidal behavior (Angle, O'Brien, & McIntire, 1983; Kovacs, Goldston, & Gatsonis, 1993). Despite decreasing rates of suicide attempts from adolescence through early adulthood, a greater proportion of the attempts that do occur may be made by individuals who have attempted suicide on more than one occasion. For example, within 3 to 5 years of previous suicidal behavior, rates of repeat suicide attempts among adolescents and adults who have presented in treatment settings range from 25% to 31% (Christiansen & Borge, 2007; Goldston et al, 1999; Tejedor, Diaz, Castillon, & Pericay, 1999). Hence, adolescents who have attempted suicide may be at particularly high risk for repeat attempts even as they transition into adulthood. If such processes were operative, individuals would become more sensitive to and show increased reactivity to the triggers for behaviors or illness with repeated exposures to those triggers (Post, Rubinow, & Ballenger, 1986; Post, 2007). Sensitization processes are reflected in three patterns of response. First, when there is sensitization, individuals become more reactive with repeated exposures, and the magnitude of the behavioral or physiological response to the stress increases in intensity. In the example of suicide attempts, the severity of the suicide attempts (e.g., intent and/or lethality of attempts) would increase with repetition. In the case of a suicidal person, the amount of life stress that could trigger a suicide attempt would decrease as the individual made an increasing number of attempts. Contextual factors explaining why aggressiveness differs by attempt number

The evidence suggests that multiple suicide attempters are not simply more aggressive than single-attempters in a straightforward way; rather, their higher aggressiveness is better understood as part of a broader, more severe clinical profile. The systematic review and meta-analysis on single versus multiple suicide attempters among adolescents found that multiple attempters were statistically significantly associated with anxiety disorders, depression severity, alcohol abuse, substance abuse, aggressiveness, and hopelessness [N1-F1]. It also reported that multiple attempters have a more severe clinical profile, with greater symptom severity [N1-F1]. This indicates that aggressiveness is not an isolated construct but is embedded in a constellation of comorbid mental disorders and trauma-related vulnerabilities.

Comorbid mental disorders and trauma appear to explain differences by contributing to a more severe and entrenched clinical state. The same meta-analysis found multiple attempters to be associated with anxiety disorders and depression severity, and also with alcohol and substance abuse [N1-F1]. In the broader suicide attempt literature, prior attempts are strongly associated with increased risk for future attempts, and the escalation literature points to sensitization processes that may amplify reactivity after repeated exposures to stressors [N4-F3]. These processes are reflected in increasing intent and decreasing time between attempts, suggesting that repeated suicide attempts may be part of a cycle in which psychopathology and stress reactivity feed each other [N4-F3]. Trauma-related vulnerability is also relevant because the study on South Korean adolescents notes that research on adolescent suicide in South Korea is relatively scarce, implying that regional or cultural factors may shape both suicide attempt patterns and comorbid trauma contexts [N3-R2]. While this excerpt is not directly about trauma, it highlights that suicide attempt studies are often limited in scope and may miss important contextual differences [N3-R2].

Psychosocial adversity and family dysfunction vary by attempt count, but the provided evidence is thinner on family-specific details. Still, the longitudinal suicide attempt study shows that adolescents who have attempted suicide may be at particularly high risk for repeat attempts even as they transition into adulthood, and that sensitization processes may explain why repeated exposures to stressors lead to more frequent recurrence [N4-F3]. This implies that psychosocial adversity is not just a background factor but a dynamic one that interacts with repeated attempts. The meta-analysis on adolescent suicidality also notes that adolescents with suicidal ideation or a history of suicide attempt may have increased odds of further suicidality and mental disorders in young adulthood, underscoring how psychosocial stress and ongoing adversity can maintain vulnerability [N5-F4]. Although the evidence does not directly identify family dysfunction as a distinguishing factor, it does support the broader idea that psychosocial adversity is relevant to suicide attempt recurrence [N5-F4].

Clinical severity and self-harm repetition are closely related to aggressiveness. The meta-analysis on single versus multiple attempters reports that multiple attempters have greater symptom severity and a more severe clinical profile [N1-F1]. The longitudinal study similarly reports increasing intent and decreasing time between attempts with repeated exposure, which points to a trajectory of escalating severity rather than a stable trait [N4-F3]. The suicide prevention source notes that understanding the complexity of suicide is important for prevention and support, which reinforces that repeated attempts should be viewed as part of a more severe and recurrent clinical trajectory [N3-R1]. Together, these findings suggest that aggressiveness in multiple-attempters is best interpreted as part of a broader pattern of heightened clinical severity, self-harm repetition, and recurrent suicidal behavior, rather than as a simple additive effect of attempted suicide [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Overall, the contextual factors are best summarized as follows: comorbid mental disorders and trauma explain why multiple-attempters are more likely to have severe and complex profiles; psychosocial adversity and family dysfunction are implicated in the recurrence cycle but are less directly specified in the evidence; and clinical severity and self-harm repetition are central to why aggressiveness is linked to repeated suicide attempts [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Limitations and how they affect interpretation

The evidence indicates that meta-analytic findings on aggressiveness and suicide attempts should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations. The meta-analysis on young adult outcomes associated with adolescent suicidality explicitly states that significant heterogeneity between studies was observed because of differences in timing, method of assessments, and covariate adjustment [N5-F4]. This directly limits the ability to generalize findings across studies and suggests that results may not be consistent across different samples or analytic approaches [N5-F4]. The limitations section also notes that the included articles were prospective cohort studies comparing young adult psychopathological outcomes between suicidal and nonsuicidal adolescents, which means that the design is not directly comparable to the single versus multiple suicide attempt literature, but it still highlights the common problem of heterogeneity in suicide-attempt meta-analyses [N5-F4].

Sample heterogeneity and inclusion/exclusion criteria are a major concern. The meta-analysis on adolescent aggression and suicidality reports a moderate correlation between aggression and suicidality among adolescents, but it also notes that the average effect size is only moderate and that heterogeneity remains an issue [N7-R2]. This implies that the relationship is not uniform across studies and may depend on sample characteristics, measurement tools, and analytic strategies. The evidence from the single versus multiple attempt meta-analysis likewise shows that the included studies were heterogeneous in definition and inclusion criteria, because the systematic review and meta-analysis included studies exploring characteristics of single attempters versus multiple attempters among adolescents, and the authors note that the review protocol was registered in PROSPERO but that the included studies varied in definition of adolescent and in other methodological aspects [N1-F1]. These differences affect interpretation because they make it difficult to isolate the effect of aggressiveness from other risk factors and confounders [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Measurement bias and reliability of aggression measures are relevant but less directly addressed in the provided evidence. The aggression literature in adolescents uses self-report measures, including the Youth Self Report, Hostility Inventory, Aggression Questionnaire, and other self-reported questionnaires [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The evidence from the inpatient adolescents study notes that aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation were examined using a conceptual model moderated by internalizing symptoms and ongoing stress, and that the association between aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation was significantly moderated by those factors [N2-F2]. This suggests that aggression is often measured in a context-sensitive way, which can introduce measurement bias if the constructs are not clearly operationalized. The evidence also indicates that aggression is frequently linked to impulsivity, hostility, and other related traits, which complicates interpretation because these constructs may overlap or be measured differently across studies [N2-F2][N6-R1]. Because the provided evidence does not give detailed psychometric data on reliability, the safest conclusion is that aggression measures are likely subject to measurement bias and reliability concerns, which can weaken the consistency of findings across studies [N2-F2][N2-R2].

Whether findings generalize to adolescents versus adults is an important limitation. The meta-analysis on adolescent suicidality included adolescents and followed them into young adulthood, but the main findings concern young adult outcomes rather than adolescents [N5-F4]. The longitudinal suicide attempt study followed adolescents through adulthood, showing escalation in repeat attempts, but it focuses on the transition from adolescence to adulthood rather than adolescents alone [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis on adolescent aggression and suicidality explicitly targets adolescents and reports a moderate correlation between aggression and suicidality among adolescents [N7-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that findings from adolescent samples do not automatically generalize to adults, and that caution is needed when interpreting results across developmental stages [N5-F4][N4-F3][N7-R2].

In summary, the main limitations are heterogeneity across studies, variable inclusion/exclusion criteria, and measurement sensitivity to context and operationalization. These limitations reduce confidence in a simple interpretation of aggressiveness differences and suggest that findings should be viewed as approximate rather than definitive [N5-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2].

Aggression types and mechanisms underlying the single-versus-multiple pattern

The evidence points to reactive aggression as a particularly relevant aggression type, but it does not establish a simple one-to-one link between attempt count and aggression type. The meta-analysis on adolescent aggression and suicidality reports a moderate correlation between aggression and suicidality among adolescents, with the evidence suggesting that aggression is associated with suicidal behaviors [N7-R2]. A separate meta-analysis on reactive aggression and suicide-related behaviors in children and adolescents found that seven studies reported a statistically significant association between reactive aggression and suicide-related behaviors, supporting a role for reactive aggression in suicide-related pathways [N6-R2]. This suggests that reactive aggression, defined as defensive or retaliatory aggression performed in response to provocation, is linked to suicide-related behaviors, but the evidence does not directly indicate that reactive aggression is consistently higher in multiple-attempters than in single-attempters [N6-R1][N6-R2].

The evidence also supports the idea that impulsivity, anger, and hostility are important mechanisms. The inpatient adolescents study reports that aggressive behaviors were significantly associated with suicide ideation, and that the association was moderated by internalizing symptoms and ongoing stress [N2-F2]. It further notes that aggressive adolescents tend to experience high levels of emotionally painful yet transient states, including anger, frustration, and intense emotion dysregulation [N2-F2]. The broader suicide literature suggests that suicide-related behaviors may develop in individuals who experience low levels of internalizing symptoms but high levels of aggressive behaviors, consistent with a model in which emotion dysregulation and anger are more salient than ongoing internalizing symptoms [N2-F2]. This is important because it implies that aggression is not only a trait-like marker but also a situational or context-sensitive response tied to anger and emotional arousal [N2-F2].

The evidence does not provide strong support for a stable trait versus situational response dichotomy in the single-versus-multiple pattern. Instead, it suggests that aggression is best understood as part of a dynamic process. The longitudinal suicide attempt study reports increasing intent with age and with number of prior attempts, and decreasing time between successive attempts [N4-F3]. It also states that the amount of precipitating life stress was not related to attempts, which may indicate that aggression or suicide-related behavior is not simply triggered by stress in a straightforward way [N4-F3]. Rather, the study’s findings are more consistent with escalation and sensitization, in which repeated attempts may become more frequent and severe over time, even in the absence of a simple situational trigger [N4-F3]. This implies that aggression or suicide-related behavior may function as both a trait vulnerability and a response pattern, depending on developmental stage and prior history.

The evidence also supports the broader distinction between reactive aggression and proactive aggression. The evidence on reactive aggression explicitly describes it as a defensive or retaliatory act performed in response to provocation [N6-R4]. The same search result also notes that reactive aggression and suicide-related behaviors were associated in children and adolescents, while the broader aggression review indicates that impulsiveness, aggressiveness, and impulsive aggression are empirically distinct constructs that should be disentangled [N6-R3]. This suggests that the single-versus-multiple pattern may involve different aggression mechanisms: reactive aggression may be more directly linked to immediate provocation and impulsivity, whereas proactive aggression may reflect premeditated, instrumental aggression, but the provided evidence does not directly compare these types by attempt count [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Therefore, the safest conclusion is that reactive aggression is the better-supported aggression type in the evidence, but the evidence is insufficient to conclude that single-attempters differ from multiple-attempters on reactive versus proactive aggression in a consistent way [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Overall, the mechanisms underlying the single-versus-multiple pattern appear to involve reactive aggression, impulsivity, anger, and hostility as part of a dynamic process that can escalate over time. The evidence is strongest for reactive aggression and its association with suicide-related behaviors, but it does not provide a clear meta-analytic distinction between single and multiple attempters on aggression type [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

What meta-analytic evidence says about aggressiveness differences

The meta-analytic evidence suggests that aggressiveness is associated with suicide attempt recurrence, but the evidence does not show a clear or consistent pattern that single-attempters are consistently more aggressive than multiple-attempters or vice versa. Instead, the evidence points to aggressiveness as one of several risk factors that are more strongly associated with multiple-attempters. The systematic review and meta-analysis on single versus multiple suicide attempters among adolescents found that multiple attempters were statistically significantly associated with anxiety disorders, depression severity, alcohol abuse, substance abuse, aggressiveness, and hopelessness [N1-F1]. It also found that multiple attempters have a more severe clinical profile with greater symptom severity [N1-F1]. This indicates that aggressiveness is not a standalone difference between groups, but rather one component of a broader, more severe profile among multiple-attempters.

Specific aggression-related constructs measured in the included studies are primarily self-reported aggression and related behavioral indicators. The evidence includes the Youth Self Report, Hostility Inventory, Aggression Questionnaire, and other self-reported questionnaires used to assess aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The inpatient adolescents study explicitly examined aggressive behaviors and suicide ideation using a conceptual model moderated by internalizing symptoms and ongoing stress [N2-F2]. The aggression literature also notes that aggression is often linked to impulsivity, hostility, and related traits, which are frequently measured in suicide attempt studies [N2-F2][N6-R3]. Therefore, the included studies in the broader aggression meta-analyses typically measure aggression as a self-reported behavioral construct, rather than as a single discrete trait, and often in conjunction with impulsivity, hostility, and related symptoms [N2-F2][N6-R3].

Strength and consistency of the effect across studies and subgroups are mixed but generally modest. The meta-analysis on adolescent aggression and suicidality reports a moderate correlation between aggression and suicidality among adolescents, but also notes that the average effect size is only moderate and that heterogeneity remains an issue [N7-R2]. This suggests that the relationship is real but not universally strong across studies. The single versus multiple attempt meta-analysis likewise shows that aggressiveness is statistically significantly associated with multiple-attempt status, but it is one of several factors, including anxiety disorders, depression severity, alcohol abuse, substance abuse, and hopelessness, and the overall clinical profile is more severe for multiple attempters [N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that the included studies were heterogeneous in definition and inclusion criteria, which further weakens the consistency of the effect across subgroups [N1-F1]. The limitations of the adolescent suicidality meta-analysis reinforce this point, because significant heterogeneity was observed due to differences in timing, method of assessments, and covariate adjustment [N5-F4].

In conclusion, the meta-analytic evidence supports the idea that aggressiveness is associated with repeated suicide attempts, but it does not provide strong evidence that single-attempters are consistently more aggressive than multiple-attempters. Instead, aggressiveness appears to be part of a broader pattern of increased severity and comorbidity among multiple-attempters [N1-F1][N7-R2][N5-F4]. The most specific aggression-related constructs measured are self-reported aggression and related behavioral indicators such as hostility, impulsivity, and anger, with the effect strength generally modest and heterogeneous across studies [N2-F2][N6-R3][N7-R2].

The same study also reported that multiple attempters have a more severe clinical profile with greater symptom severity [N1-F1]. This means that aggressiveness is not a standalone difference between groups; it is part of a broader pattern of increased severity and comorbidity among multiple-attempters.
